=== Vertical axis ===
[[File:Quietrevolution Bristol 3513051949.jpg|thumb|A small [[Quietrevolution wind turbine|Quietrevolution QR5]] <!--no link: [[MOS:SOB]]-->Gorlov-type vertical-axis wind turbine on top of the [[Bristol Beacon]] in [[Bristol]], England. Measuring 3 m in diameter and 5 m high, it has a [[Nameplate capacity|nameplate rating]] of 6.5 kW to the grid.]]
[[Vertical-axis wind turbine]]s (or VAWTs) have the main rotor shaft arranged vertically. One advantage of this arrangement is that the turbine does not need to be pointed into the wind to be effective,<ref name="auto">{{cite journal |last1=Tummala |first1=Abhishiktha |last2=Velamati |first2=Ratna Kishore |last3=Sinha |first3=Dipankur Kumar |last4=Indraja |first4=V. |last5=Krishna |first5=V. Hari |title=A review on small scale wind turbines |journal=Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews |date=April 2016 |volume=56 |pages=1351–1371 |doi=10.1016/j.rser.2015.12.027 |bibcode=2016RSERv..56.1351T }}</ref> which is an advantage on a site where the wind direction is highly variable. It is also an advantage when the turbine is integrated into a building because it is inherently less steerable. Also, the generator and gearbox can be placed near the ground, using a direct drive from the rotor assembly to the ground-based gearbox, improving accessibility for maintenance. However, these designs produce much less energy averaged over time, which is a major drawback.<ref name="wind-works.org"/><ref>{{cite web |url=http://cleantechnica.com/2014/04/07/vertical-axis-wind-turbines-great-1890-also-rans-2014/ |website=[[CleanTechnica]]|title=Vertical Axis Wind Turbines: Great In 1890, Also-rans In 2014 |date=7 April 2014 |author=Michael Barnard}}</ref>

Vertical turbine designs have much lower efficiency than standard horizontal designs.<ref>{{cite book |last=Hau |first=E. |title=Wind Turbines: Fundamentals, Technologies, Application, Economics |publisher=Springer |location=Germany |year=2006 |doi=10.1007/3-540-29284-5 |isbn=978-3-540-24240-6<!--doi and isbn according to ResearchGate-->}}</ref> The key disadvantages include the relatively low rotational speed with the consequential higher [[torque]] and hence higher cost of the drive train, the inherently lower [[Wind turbine aerodynamics#Power Coefficient|power coefficient]], the 360-degree rotation of the aerofoil within the wind flow during each cycle and hence the highly dynamic loading on the blade, the pulsating torque generated by some rotor designs on the drive train, and the difficulty of modelling the wind flow accurately and hence the challenges of analysing and designing the rotor prior to fabricating a prototype.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.awsopenwind.org/downloads/documentation/ModelingUncertaintyPublic.pdf |title=Wind Flow Modeling Uncertainty |date=May 2010 |publisher=AWS Truepower |first1=Michael C. |last1=Brower |first2=Nicholas M. |last2=Robinson |first3=Erik |last3=Hale |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130502230520/http://www.awsopenwind.org/downloads/documentation/ModelingUncertaintyPublic.pdf |archive-date=2013-05-02}}</ref>

When a turbine is mounted on a rooftop the building generally redirects wind over the roof and this can double the wind speed at the turbine. If the height of a rooftop-mounted turbine tower is about half of the building height it is near the optimum for maximum wind energy and minimum wind turbulence. While wind speeds within the built environment are generally much lower than at exposed rural sites, noise may be a concern and an existing structure must be able to resist the additional stress.<ref>{{cite web |last=Piggott |first=Hugh |date=6 January 2007 |title=Windspeed in the city – reality versus the DTI database |url=https://www.scoraigwind.com/citywinds |access-date=6 November 2013 |website=Hugh Piggott's blog}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.urbanwind.net/pdf/technological_analysis.pdf |title=Urban Wind Turbines Technology Review |publisher=Wineur |access-date=24 August 2011|archive-date=30 May 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090530012822/http://www.urbanwind.net/pdf/technological_analysis.pdf |url-status=dead}}</ref>{{fcn|reason=Unclear who wrote this|date=September 2026}}

There are several subtypes of the vertical-axis design, including the [[Darrieus wind turbine]], also known as an eggbeater turbine. These were named for [[Georges Jean Marie Darrieus]] who patented a design in the 1920s. They have good efficiency, but produce large [[torque ripple]] and cyclical stress on the tower, which contributes to poor reliability. The torque ripple is reduced by using three or more blades, which results in greater solidity of the rotor.<!-- Solidity is measured by the blade area divided by the rotor area. WD NEED ADDIT SRC--><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Möllerström |first1=Erik |last2=Gipe |first2=Paul |last3=Beurskens |first3=Jos |last4=Ottermo |first4=Fredric |title=A historical review of vertical axis wind turbines rated 100 kW and above |journal=Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews |date=May 2019 |volume=105 |pages=1–13 |doi=10.1016/j.rser.2018.12.022 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019RSERv.105....1M }}</ref> The giromill is a subtype of Darrieus turbine with straight blades. The cycloturbine variety has variable pitch to reduce the torque pulsation and is self-starting.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.awea.org/faq/vawt.html |title=What Are Vertical-Axis Wind Turbines (VAWTs)? |first1=Eric |last1=Eggleston |name-list-style=amp |display-authors=etal<!--AWEA Staff--> |publisher=American Wind Energy Association |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050403101826/http://www.awea.org/faq/vawt.html |archive-date=3 April 2005}}</ref> The advantages of variable pitch are high starting torque; a wide, relatively flat torque curve; a higher [[coefficient of performance]]; more efficient operation in turbulent winds; and a lower blade speed ratio, which lowers blade bending stresses. Straight, V, or curved blades may be used.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marloff |first=Richard H. |date=1978 |title=Stresses in turbine-blade tenons subjected to bending |journal=Experimental Mechanics |volume=18 |issue=1 |pages=19–24 |doi=10.1007/BF02326553  }}</ref>

[[File:Twisted Savonius wind turbine in operation@60rpm.gif|thumb|upright=0.75<!--Don't use both upright and a pixel size. They're redundant. Prefer upright-->|A vertical-axis twisted-Savonius-type turbine]]

The Savonius wind turbine are drag-type devices with two (or more) scoops that are used in anemometers, ''Flettner'' vents (commonly seen on bus and van roofs), and in some high-reliability low-efficiency power turbines. They are always self-starting if there are at least three scoops.<ref name="auto"/> Twisted Savonius is a modified Savonius with long helical scoops to provide smooth torque. This is often used as a rooftop wind turbine and has even been [[Hornblower Hybrid|adapted for ships]].<ref>{{cite news |first=Rob |last=Varnon |url=http://www.ctpost.com/news/article/Derecktor-converting-boat-into-hybrid-passenger-851170.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101204124008/http://www.ctpost.com/news/article/Derecktor-converting-boat-into-hybrid-passenger-851170.php |archive-date=4 December 2010 |title=Derecktor converting boat into hybrid passenger ferry |website=Connecticut Post |date=2 December 2010 |access-date=25 April 2012 }}</ref> [[Airborne wind turbines]] consist of wings or a small aircraft tethered to the ground.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cherubini |first1=Antonello |last2=Papini |first2=Andrea |last3=Vertechy |first3=Rocco |last4=Fontana |first4=Marco |title=Airborne Wind Energy Systems: A review of the technologies |journal=Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews |date=November 2015 |volume=51 |pages=1461–1476 |doi=10.1016/j.rser.2015.07.053 |bibcode=2015RSERv..51.1461C |hdl=11382/503316 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> They are useful for reaching faster winds above which traditional turbines can operate. There are prototypes in operation in east Africa.<ref>{{Cite web |title=After a Shaky Start, Airborne Wind Energy Is Slowly Taking Off |url=https://e360.yale.edu/features/after-a-shaky-start-airborne-wind-energy-is-slowly-taking-off |access-date=2023-06-02 |website=Yale E360 |language=en-US}}</ref> A [[floating wind turbine]] is an offshore turbine supported by a floating platform.<ref>{{Cite web |title=So, What Exactly Is Floating Offshore Wind? |url=https://www.greentechmedia.com/articles/read/so-what-exactly-floating-offshore-wind |access-date=2023-06-02 |website=Greentech Media}}</ref> By having them float, they can to be installed in deeper water, allowing more of them; by having them further out of sight from land, they may create less public concern about their visual impact.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-12-16 |title=The US has just started building floating wind turbines – how do they work? |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2022/12/floating-wind-turbines-us/ |access-date=2023-06-02 |publisher=World Economic Forum}}</ref>

== Design and construction ==

{{Main|Wind turbine design}}

[[File:EERE illust large turbine.gif|thumb|Components of a horizontal-axis wind turbine]]

[[File:WKA spannglieder.jpg|thumb|Inside view of a wind turbine tower, showing the tendon cables]]

===Components===

Wind turbines convert wind energy to electrical energy for distribution. Conventional horizontal-axis turbines can be divided into three components:

* The rotor, which is approximately 20% of the wind turbine cost, includes the blades for converting wind energy to low-speed rotational energy.<ref name=":4"/>
* The generator, which is approximately 34% of the wind turbine cost, includes the [[electrical generator]],<ref>{{cite journal |journal=International Journal of Dynamics and Control |title=A Review on the Development of the Wind Turbine Generators across the World |author=Navid Goudarzi |date=June 2013 |volume=1 |issue=2 |pages=192–202 |doi=10.1007/s40435-013-0016-y|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |journal=ASME 2012 International Mechanical Engineering Congress and Exposition |title=A Review of the Development of Wind Turbine Generators Across the World |author1=Navid Goudarzi |author2=Weidong Zhu |date=November 2012 |volume=4 – Paper No: IMECE2012-88615 |pages=1257–1265 |url=http://proceedings.asmedigitalcollection.asme.org/proceeding.aspx?articleid=1750788}}</ref> the control electronics, and most likely a [[gearbox]] (e.g., [[epicyclic gearing|planetary gear box]]),<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.hansentransmissions.com/en/hansen_w4.html |title=Hansen W4 series |publisher=Hansentransmissions.com |access-date=6 November 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120315160450/http://www.hansentransmissions.com/en/hansen_w4.html |archive-date=15 March 2012}}</ref> [[adjustable-speed drive]], or [[continuously variable transmission]] to convert the low-speed incoming rotation to high-speed rotation suitable for generating electricity.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://coen.boisestate.edu/windenergy/files/2011/10/Active-Drivetrain-Control-to-Improve-Energy-Capture-of-Wind-Turbines.pdf |title=Active Drivetrain Control to Improve Energy Capture of Wind Turbines |first1=John |last1=Gardner |first2=Nathaniel |last2=Haro |first3=Todd |last3=Haynes |date=October 2011 |publisher=Boise State University |access-date=28 February 2012 |archive-date=7 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120307083009/http://coen.boisestate.edu/windenergy/files/2011/10/Active-Drivetrain-Control-to-Improve-Energy-Capture-of-Wind-Turbines.pdf }}</ref>
* The surrounding structure, which is approximately 15% of the wind turbine cost, includes the tower and rotor yaw mechanism.<ref name=":4">{{cite web |title="Wind Turbine Design Cost and Scaling Model", Technical Report NREL/TP-500-40566, December, 2006, page 35, 36 |url=http://www.nrel.gov/docs/fy07osti/40566.pdf |access-date=6 November 2013 |publisher=National Renewable Energy Laboratory}}</ref>

[[File:Badaia - Parque Eólico -BT- 01.jpg|thumb|[[Nacelle (wind turbine)|Nacelle]] of a wind turbine]]

A 1.5 ([[megawatt|MW]]) wind turbine of a type frequently seen in the United States has a tower {{convert|80|m|sp=us}} high. The rotor assembly (blades and hub) measures about {{Convert|80|m|ft|sp=us}} in diameter.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bauer |first=Lucas |title=GE General Electric GE 1.5s – 1,50 MW – Wind turbine |url=https://en.wind-turbine-models.com/turbines/565-ge-general-electric-ge-1.5s |access-date=2023-05-23 |website=en.wind-turbine-models.com}}</ref> The [[Nacelle (wind turbine)|nacelle]], which contains the generator, is {{Convert|15.24|m|ft|sp=us}} and weighs around 300 tons.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nacelles {{!}} How are they manufactured? |url=https://www.windpowerengineering.com/how-is-a-nacelle-manufactured/ |access-date=2023-05-23 |website=Windpower Engineering & Development}}</ref>

=== Turbine monitoring and diagnostics ===

{{see also|Wind turbine prognostics}}

Due to data transmission problems, [[structural health monitoring]] of wind turbines is usually performed using several accelerometers and strain gages attached to the nacelle to monitor the gearbox and equipment. Currently, [[Digital image correlation for electronics|digital image correlation]] and [[Photogrammetry|stereophotogrammetry]] are used to measure dynamics of wind turbine blades. These methods usually measure displacement and strain to identify location of defects. Dynamic characteristics of non-rotating wind turbines have been measured using digital image correlation and photogrammetry.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.ymssp.2015.03.021 |volume=62–63 |title=Full-field dynamic strain prediction on a wind turbine using displacements of optical targets measured by stereophotogrammetry |year=2015 |journal=Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing |pages=284–295 |last1=Baqersad |first1=Javad |last2=Niezrecki |first2=Christopher |last3=Avitabile |first3=Peter |bibcode=2015MSSP...62..284B }}</ref> Three dimensional point tracking has also been used to measure rotating dynamics of wind turbines.<ref>{{Cite book |chapter=Using High-Speed Stereophotogrammetry Techniques to Extract Shape Information from Wind Turbine/Rotor Operating Data |first1=Troy |title=Topics in Modal Analysis II, Volume 6|last1=Lundstrom |first2=Javad |last2=Baqersad |first3=Christopher |last3=Niezrecki |first4=Peter |last4=Avitabile |editor-first1=R. |editor-last1=Allemang |editor-first2=J.|editor-last2=De Clerck|editor-first3=C. |editor-last3=Niezrecki |editor-first4=J.R. |editor-last4=Blough |date=4 November 2012|publisher=Springer New York|pages=269–275 |doi=10.1007/978-1-4614-2419-2_26 |series=Conference Proceedings of the Society for Experimental Mechanics Series |isbn=978-1-4614-2418-5}}</ref>

== Technology ==

[[File:Growing size of wind turbines.png|thumb|350px|Development in size and power of wind turbines, 1990–2016]]

Generally, efficiency increases along with turbine blade lengths. The blades must be stiff, strong, durable, light and resistant to fatigue.<ref name="citeseerx.ist.psu.edu">{{Citation|last1=Ancona|first1=Dan |last2=Jim|first2=McVeigh |title=Wind Turbine – Materials and Manufacturing Fact Sheet|year=2001 |citeseerx=10.1.1.464.5842 }}</ref> Materials with these properties include composites such as polyester and epoxy, while glass fiber and carbon fiber have been used for the reinforcing.<ref name=WS2010>{{cite web |last1=Watson |first1=James |last2=Serrano |first2=Juan |title=Composite Materials for Wind Blades |url=http://www.windsystemsmag.com/article/detail/149/composite-materials-for-wind-blades |website=Wind Systems |date=September 2010 |access-date=6 November 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171111041624/http://www.windsystemsmag.com/article/detail/149/composite-materials-for-wind-blades |archive-date=11 November 2017 }}</ref> Construction may involve manual layup or injection molding. Retrofitting existing turbines with larger blades reduces the task and risks of redesign.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Jossi |first=Frank |date=2021-02-04 |title=Wind developers are retrofitting newer projects with bigger, better blades |url=https://energynews.us/2021/02/04/wind-developers-are-retrofitting-newer-projects-with-bigger-better-blades/ |access-date=2023-06-02 |website=Energy News Network |language=en-US}}</ref>

While turbines have an average lifespan of 30 years, blades and gearboxes usually last up to 25 years.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The average lifespan of wind turbines may surprise you |url=https://www.slashgear.com/2110775/wind-turbines-average-lifespan/ |access-date=2026-03-17 |website=slashgear.com |date=2026-03-02}}</ref>

=== Blade materials ===

Materials commonly used in wind turbine blades are described below.

==== Glass and carbon fibers ====

[[File:Turbine Blade Convoy Passing through Edenfield.jpg|thumb|A [[Wind turbine design#Blades|turbine blade]] convoy passing through [[Edenfield]], England]]
The stiffness of composites is determined by the stiffness of fibers and their volume content. Typically, E-glass fibers are used as main reinforcement in the composites. Typically, the glass/epoxy composites for wind turbine blades contain up to 75% glass by weight. This increases the stiffness, tensile and compression strength. A promising composite material is glass fiber with modified compositions like S-glass, R-glass etc. Other glass fibers developed by Owens Corning are ECRGLAS, Advantex and WindStrand.<ref>{{Cite web |url= http://windpower.sandia.gov/other/AIAA-092449C.pdf |title= Materials and Innovations for Large Blade Structures: Research Opportunities in Wind Energy Technology |website= windpower.sandia.gov |access-date= 27 February 2018 |archive-date= 13 August 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170813063425/http://windpower.sandia.gov/other/AIAA-092449C.pdf }}</ref>

Carbon fiber has more tensile strength, higher stiffness and lower density than glass fiber. An ideal candidate for these properties is the spar cap, a structural element of a blade that experiences high tensile loading.<ref name=WS2010/> A {{convert|100|m|adj=on}} glass fiber blade could weigh up to {{convert|50|t|lb}}, while using carbon fiber in the spar saves 20% to 30% weight, about {{convert|15|t|lb}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url= http://www.compositesworld.com/articles/wind-turbine-blades-glass-vs-carbon-fiber|title=Wind turbine blades: Glass vs. carbon fiber |website=www.compositesworld.com |access-date=12 November 2016}}</ref>

==== Hybrid reinforcements ====
Instead of making wind turbine blade reinforcements from pure glass or pure carbon, hybrid designs trade weight for cost. For example, for an {{convert|8|m|adj=on}} blade, a full replacement by carbon fiber would save 80% of weight but increase costs by 150%, while a 30% replacement would save 50% of weight and increase costs by 90%. Hybrid reinforcement materials include E-glass/carbon, E-glass/aramid. The current longest blade by LM Wind Power is made of carbon/glass hybrid composites. More research is needed about the optimal composition of materials.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.windpowermonthly.com/article/1419306|title=Turbines of the year: Rotor blades|first=Eize de|last=Vries|website=www.windpowermonthly.com}}</ref>

==== Nano-engineered polymers and composites ====
Additions of small amount (0.5 weight %) of nanoreinforcement ([[carbon nanotubes]] or nanoclay) in the polymer matrix of composites, fiber sizing or inter-laminar layers can improve fatigue resistance, shear or compressive strength, and fracture toughness of the composites by 30% to 80%. Research has also shown that incorporating small amounts of carbon nanotubes (CNT) can increase the lifetime up to 1500%.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1109/ICASET.2019.8714217 |chapter=Nanoengineered Composite Materials for Wind Turbine Blades |title=2019 Advances in Science and Engineering Technology International Conferences (ASET) |date=2019 |last1=Panduranga |first1=Raghu |last2=Alamoudi |first2=Yasser |last3=Ferrah |first3=Azzeddine |pages=1–7 |isbn=978-1-5386-8271-5 }}</ref>

=== Costs ===
The global weighted average [[capital cost]] of a wind turbine was approximately $2,324 per kilowatt in 2010. {{as of|2024}}, this figure had fallen to $1,041 per [[nameplate capacity|kilowatt of nameplate capacity]], reflecting a consistent year-on-year decline of around 12%.<ref name="irena">{{cite report |author=[[International Renewable Energy Agency]] |title=Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024 |publisher=International Renewable Energy Agency |year=2025 |url=https://www.irena.org/-/media/Files/IRENA/Agency/Publication/2025/Jul/IRENA_TEC_RPGC_in_2024_2025.pdf |access-date=13 March 2026}}</ref> [[Home wind turbine]]s are significantly cheaper, with costs as little as $700 for a small 400 W turbine (non-including installation costs) in the U.S.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wind Turbine Cost Guide 2025: Complete Pricing Breakdown ($700-$20M+) |url=https://solartechonline.com/blog/wind-turbine-cost-guide-2025/ |website=solartechonline.com |access-date=13 March 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260211004739/https://solartechonline.com/blog/wind-turbine-cost-guide-2025/ |archive-date=11 February 2026 |date=19 October 2025}}</ref>

The [[levelized cost of energy]] (LCOE) of wind turbines, or the average minimum price per unit of energy a power plant must receive to break even over its lifetime, as of 2025 spanned from $25 per MWh in China to $70 per MWh in [[Vietnam]], and averaged globally around $50–60 per MWh.<ref>{{cite web |title=Renewable levelized cost of electricity competitiveness reaches new milestone across global markets in 2025 |url=https://www.woodmac.com/press-releases/renewable-levelized-cost-of-electricity-competitiveness-reaches-new-milestone-across-global-markets-in-2025/ |publisher=Wood Mackenzie |access-date=13 March 2026 |date=22 October 2025}}</ref> The [[MENA]] region reported the lowest average LCOE, with the 2024 [[Al Ghat wind farm]] project in [[Saudi Arabia]] setting a global record of only $15.66 per MWh.<ref>{{cite web |title=Saudi Arabia sets world record for lowest cost of electricity from wind power |url=https://www.zawya.com/en/projects/utilities/saudi-arabia-sets-world-record-for-lowest-cost-of-electricity-from-wind-power-xxry6l26 |website=zany.com |access-date=13 March 2026 |date=21 May 2024}}</ref>

For the wind turbine blades, while the material cost is much higher for hybrid glass/carbon fiber blades than all-glass fiber blades, labor costs can be lower. Using carbon fiber allows simpler designs that use less raw material. The chief manufacturing process in blade fabrication is the layering of plies. Thinner blades allow reducing the number of layers and thus the labor and in some cases, equate to the cost of labor for glass fiber blades.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Ong |first1=Cheng-Huat |last2=Tsai |first2=Stephen W. |name-list-style=amp |date=1 Mar 2000 |title=The Use of Carbon Fibers in Wind Turbine Blade Design |url=http://energy.sandia.gov/wp-content/gallery/uploads/SAND2000-0478.pdf |website=energy.sandia.gov}}</ref>

Offshore has significantly higher installation costs.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Onshore vs offshore wind energy: what's the difference? |publisher=National Grid Group |url=https://www.nationalgrid.com/stories/energy-explained/onshore-vs-offshore-wind-energy |access-date=2023-05-23 }}</ref> The global weighted average total installation costs for offshore turbines were $2,852 per kW in 2024, having fallen by 48% from the 2010 costs of $5,518 per kW.<ref name="irena" />

=== Non-blade materials ===

Wind turbine parts other than the rotor blades (including the rotor hub, gearbox, frame, and tower) are largely made of steel. Smaller turbines (as well as megawatt-scale Enercon turbines) have begun using aluminum alloys for these components to make turbines lighter and more efficient. This trend may grow if fatigue and strength properties can be improved. Pre-stressed concrete has been increasingly used for the material of the tower, but still requires much reinforcing steel to meet the strength requirement of the turbine. Additionally, step-up gearboxes are being increasingly replaced with variable speed generators, which requires magnetic materials.<ref name="citeseerx.ist.psu.edu"/>

Modern turbines use some [[Copper in renewable energy#Wind|two tons of copper]] for [[wiring]], generators, transformers, and [[grounding system]]s<ref>Frost and Sullivan, 2009, cited in Wind Generator Technology, by Eclareon S.L., Madrid, May 2012; www.eclareon.com; Available at Leonardo Energy – Ask an Expert; {{cite web |author=Fernando Nuno |date=2012-05-30 |url=http://www.leonardo-energy.org/ask-expert |title=Ask an expert |website=Leonardo ENERGY |access-date=2012-12-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121126131037/http://www.leonardo-energy.org/ask-expert |archive-date=26 November 2012 }}</ref> due to its exceptional electrical conductivity
and durability.<ref name="jrc">{{cite report |last1=Carrara |first1=S. |last2=Baldassarre |first2=B. |last3=Jakimow |first3=M. |last4=Kuzov |first4=T. |last5=Mc Govern |first5=L. |display-authors=et al. |editor-last=Black |editor-first=C. |title=Deep Dive on Critical Raw Materials for Wind Turbines in the EU |publisher=Publications Office of the European Union |location=Luxembourg |year=2025 |id=JRC141759 |doi=10.2760/5665594 |url=https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2760/5665594}}</ref> {{as of|2018}}, global production of wind turbines use {{convert|450,000|t|e6lb|abbr=off}} of copper per year.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fast pace of growth in wind energy driving demand for copper |url=https://www.rivieramm.com/editors-choice-brand/fast-pace-of-growth-in-wind-energy-driving-demand-for-copper-56058 |website=Riviera Maritime Media}}</ref> As of 2025, copper intensity ranges between 650 and 6,200 kg per MW of capacity.<ref name="jrc" />

=== Material supply ===
[[File:Nordex Jonesboro Plant 001.jpg|thumb|[[Nordex]] wind turbine manufacturing plant in [[Jonesboro, Arkansas|Jonesboro]], Arkansas, United States]]
A 2015 study of the material consumption trends and requirements for wind energy in Europe found that bigger turbines have a higher consumption of precious metals but lower material input per [[Kilowatt|kW]] generated. The material consumption and stock at that time was compared to input materials for various onshore system sizes. In all EU countries, the estimates for 2020 doubled the values consumed in 2009. These countries would need to expand their resources to meet the estimated demand for 2020. For example, the EU had 3% of world supply of [[fluorspar]], and it would require 14% by 2020. Globally, the main exporting countries are South Africa, Mexico, and China. This is similar to other critical and valuable materials required for energy systems such as magnesium, silver and indium. While the levels of recycling of these materials are very low, focusing on their [[Circular economy|circularity]] could alleviate supply. Since most of these valuable materials are also used in other emerging technologies, like [[light emitting diode]]s (LEDs), [[photo voltaics]] (PVs) and [[liquid crystal display]]s (LCDs), their demand is expected to grow.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=Junbeum |last2=Guillaume |first2=Bertrand |last3=Chung |first3=Jinwook |last4=Hwang |first4=Yongwoo |title=Critical and precious materials consumption and requirement in wind energy system in the EU 27 |journal=Applied Energy |date=February 2015 |volume=139 |pages=327–334 |doi=10.1016/j.apenergy.2014.11.003 |bibcode=2015ApEn..139..327K }}</ref>

A 2011 study by the United States Geological Survey estimated resources required to fulfill the US commitment to supplying 20% of its electricity from wind power by 2030. It did not consider requirements for small turbines or offshore turbines because those were not common in 2008 when the study was done. Common materials such as cast iron, steel and concrete would increase by 2%–3% compared to 2008. Between 110,000 and 115,000 metric tons of fiber glass would be required per year, a 14% increase. Rare-earth metal use would not increase much compared to available supply, however rare-earth metals that are also used for other technologies such as batteries which are increasing its global demand need to be taken into account. Land required would be 50,000 square kilometers onshore and 11,000 offshore. This would not be a problem in the US due to its vast area and because the same land can be used for farming. A greater challenge would be the variability and transmission to areas of high demand.<ref name="wilburn">{{cite book |last1=Wilburn |first1=David R. |url=https://pubs.usgs.gov/sir/2011/5036/sir2011-5036.pdf |title=Wind Energy in the United States and Materials Required for the Land-Based Wind Turbine Industry from 2010 through 2030 (Scientific Investigations Report 2011-5036) |date=2011 |publisher=USGS |access-date=15 January 2023}}</ref>

Permanent magnets for wind turbine generators contain rare-earth metals such as [[neodymium]] (Nd), [[praseodymium]] (Pr), [[terbium]] (Tb), and [[dysprosium]] (Dy). Systems that use magnetic direct drive turbines require greater amounts of rare-earth metals. Therefore, an increase in wind turbine manufacture would increase the demand for these resources. By 2035, the demand for Nd is estimated to increase by 4,000 to 18,000 tons and for Dy by 200 to 1,200 tons. These values are a quarter to half of current production. However, these estimates are very uncertain because technologies are developing rapidly.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Buchholz |first1=Peter |last2=Brandenburg |first2=Torsten |title=Demand, Supply, and Price Trends for Mineral Raw Materials Relevant to the Renewable Energy Transition Wind Energy, Solar Photovoltaic Energy, and Energy Storage |journal=Chemie Ingenieur Technik |date=January 2018 |volume=90 |issue=1–2 |pages=141–153 |doi=10.1002/cite.201700098 }}</ref>

Reliance on [[rare earth mineral]]s for components has risked expense and price volatility as China has been main producer of rare earth minerals (96% in 2009) and was reducing its export quotas.<ref name=wilburn /> However, in recent years, other producers have increased production and China has increased export quotas, leading to higher supply, lower cost, and greater viability of large-scale use of variable-speed generators.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/china-ends-rare-earth-minerals-export-quotas-1420441285 |title=China Ends Rare-Earth Minerals Export Quotas|last1=Yap|first1=Chui-Wei |newspaper=Wall Street Journal|date=5 January 2015 }}</ref>

Glass fiber is the most common material for reinforcement. Its demand has grown due to growth in construction, transportation and wind turbines. Its global market might reach US$17.4 billion by 2024, compared to US$8.5 billion in 2014. In 2014, Asia Pacific produced more than 45% of the market; now China is the largest producer. The industry receives subsidies from the Chinese government allowing it to export cheaper to the US and Europe. However, price wars have led to anti-dumping measures such as tariffs on Chinese glass fiber.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Glass fiber market to reach to US$17 billion by 2024 |journal=Reinforced Plastics |date=July 2016 |volume=60 |issue=4 |pages=188–189 |doi=10.1016/j.repl.2016.07.006 }}</ref>

== Wind turbines on public display ==
{{Main|Wind turbines on public display}}[[File:Lamma wind turbine.jpg|thumb|The [[Nordex SE|Nordex]] N50 wind turbine and visitor centre of [[Lamma Winds]] in [[Hong Kong]], China|224x224px]]
[[File:Bahrain World Trade Center from below.jpg|thumb|218x218px|Wind turbines in the Bahrain World Trade Center]]
A few localities have exploited the attention-getting nature of wind turbines by placing them on public display, either with visitor centers around their bases, or with viewing areas farther away.<ref name="wind_farm_tourism">{{cite web |url=http://www.canada.com/edmontonjournal/news/business/story.html?id=63a5438a-ae99-4b76-9629-b7b59d238932 |title=Canada wind farms blow away turbine tourists |website=[[Edmonton Journal]] |access-date=6 September 2008 |last=Young |date=3 August 2007 |first=Kathryn |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20090425064111/http://www2.canada.com/edmontonjournal/news/business/story.html?id=63a5438a-ae99-4b76-9629-b7b59d238932 |archive-date=25 April 2009 }}</ref> The wind turbines are generally of conventional horizontal-axis, three-bladed design and generate power to feed electrical grids, but they also serve the unconventional roles of technology demonstration, public relations, and education.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rudgard |first=Olivia |date=2023-02-20 |title=Despite perception as eyesore, wind turbine tourism takes off |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2023/02/20/business/wind-turbine-tourism/ |access-date=2023-06-02 |website=The Japan Times}}</ref> The [[Bahrain World Trade Center]] has wind turbines displayed prominently for the public. It is the first skyscraper to integrate wind turbines into its design.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.norwin.dk/specialapplicati.html |title=Special Applications |publisher=Norwin A/S |access-date=2018-04-06}}</ref>

== Small wind turbines ==
{{Main|Small wind turbine}}Small wind turbines may be used for a variety of applications including on- or off-grid residences, telecom towers, offshore platforms, rural schools and clinics, remote monitoring and other purposes that require energy where there is no electric grid, or where the grid is unstable. Small wind turbines may be as small as a fifty-watt generator for boat or [[Travel trailer|caravan]] use. Hybrid solar- and wind-powered units are increasingly being used for traffic signage, particularly in rural locations, since they avoid the need to lay long cables from the nearest mains connection point.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.solar-wind.co.uk/solar_powered_sign_lights.html |title=Solar & Wind Powered Sign Lighting |last=Anon |publisher=Energy Development Cooperative Ltd |access-date=19 October 2013}}</ref> The [[National Renewable Energy Laboratory|U.S. Department of Energy's National Renewable Energy Laboratory]] (NREL) defines small wind turbines as those smaller than or equal to 100 kilowatts.<ref>[http://www.nrel.gov/wind/smallwind/ Small Wind] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111115044040/http://www.nrel.gov/wind/smallwind/ |date=15 November 2011 }}, U.S. Department of Energy National Renewable Energy Laboratory website</ref> Small units often have direct-drive generators, [[direct current]] output, aeroelastic blades, and lifetime bearings and use a vane to point into the wind.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Castellano |first=Robert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RUqXHr3WjOIC&dq=Small+units+often+have+direct+drive+generators%2C+direct+current+output%2C+aeroelastic+blades%2C+lifetime+bearings+and+use+a+vane+to+point+into+the+wind&pg=PA48 |title=Alternative Energy Technologies: Opportunities and Markets |date=2012 |publisher=Archives contemporaines |isbn=978-2-8130-0076-7 |language=en}}</ref>

== Wind turbine spacing ==

On most horizontal wind turbine farms, a spacing of about 6–10 times the rotor diameter is often upheld. However, for large wind farms, distances of about 15 rotor diameters should be more economical, taking into account typical wind turbine and land costs. This conclusion has been reached by research conducted by [[Charles Meneveau]] of Johns Hopkins University<ref>{{cite web |title=New study yields better turbine spacing for large wind farms |url=http://gazette.jhu.edu/2011/01/18/new-study-yields-better-turbine-spacing-for-large-wind-farms/ |publisher=Johns Hopkins University |date=18 January 2011 |access-date=6 November 2013}}</ref> and Johan Meyers of Leuven University in Belgium, based on computer simulations<ref>{{cite journal |author1=M. Calaf |author2=C. Meneveau |author3=J. Meyers |title=Large eddy simulation study of fully developed wind-turbine array boundary layers |date=2010 |journal=Phys. Fluids |volume=22 |issue=1 |pages = 015110–015110–16|doi=10.1063/1.3291077 |bibcode=2010PhFl...22a5110C |url=https://lirias.kuleuven.be/handle/123456789/260110 |doi-access=free }}</ref> that take into account the detailed interactions among wind turbines (wakes) as well as with the entire turbulent atmospheric boundary layer.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1002/we.469 |volume=15 |issue=2 |title=Optimal turbine spacing in fully developed wind farm boundary layers |year=2011 |journal=Wind Energy |pages=305–317 |last1=Meyers |first1=Johan|doi-access=free | bibcode=2012WiEn...15..305M |url=https://lirias.kuleuven.be/handle/123456789/331240 }}</ref>

Research by John Dabiri of Caltech suggests that vertical wind turbines may be placed much more closely together so long as an alternating pattern of rotation is created allowing blades of neighbouring turbines to move in the same direction as they approach one another.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Potential order-of-magnitude enhancement of wind farm power density via counter-rotating vertical-axis wind turbine arrays|first=John O.|last=Dabiri |date=July 2011|journal=Journal of Renewable and Sustainable Energy|volume=3|issue=4|article-number=043104 |doi=10.1063/1.3608170|arxiv = 1010.3656 }}</ref>

== Operability ==
[[File:Wind turbine maintenance (51689968067).jpg|thumb|upright|Workers inspect wind turbine blades.]]

=== Maintenance ===
Wind turbines need regular [[Maintenance, repair and operations|maintenance]] to stay [[Reliability engineering|reliable]] and [[Availability factor|available]]. In the best case turbines are available to generate energy 98% of the time.<ref>{{cite web |first1=G.J.W. |last1=van Bussel  |first2=M.B. |last2=Zaaijer  |url=https://www.ecn.nl/fileadmin/ecn/units/wind/docs/dowec/2001-MAREC-RAMS.pdf |title=Reliability, Availability and Maintenance aspects of large-scale offshore wind farms |page=2 |publisher=[[Delft University of Technology]] |year=2001  |access-date=30 May 2016 |archive-date=12 April 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160412165430/https://www.ecn.nl/fileadmin/ecn/units/wind/docs/dowec/2001-MAREC-RAMS.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://analysis.windenergyupdate.com/operations-maintenance/iberwind-builds-98-availability-fresh-yaw-blade-gains |title=Iberwind builds on 98% availability with fresh yaw, blade gains |date=15 February 2016 |access-date=30 May 2016}}</ref> Ice accretion on turbine blades has been found to greatly reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, which is a common challenge in cold climates where [[Atmospheric icing|in-cloud icing and freezing rain]] events occur.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barber |first1=S. |last2=Wang |first2=Y. |last3=Jafari |first3=S. |last4=Chokani |first4=N. |last5=Abhari |first5=R. S. |title=The Impact of Ice Formation on Wind Turbine Performance and Aerodynamics |journal=Journal of Solar Energy Engineering |date=February 2011 |volume=133 |issue=1 |article-number=011007 |doi=10.1115/1.4003187 }}</ref> [[Deicing]] is mainly performed by internal heating<ref>{{cite web |last1=Nilsen |first1=Jannicke |title=Her spyler helikopteret bort et tykt lag med is |url=https://www.tu.no/artikler/her-spyler-helikopteret-bort-et-tykt-lag-med-is/222975 |website=Tu.no |publisher=[[Teknisk Ukeblad]] |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210120061008/https://www.tu.no/artikler/her-spyler-helikopteret-bort-et-tykt-lag-med-is/222975 |archive-date=20 January 2021 |language=no |date=1 February 2015 |url-status=live |quote=These work .. by blowing hot air into the rotor blades so that the ice melts, or by using heating cables on the front edge of the rotor blades where the ice sticks. No chemicals are added to the water, in contrast to aircraft de-icing, which often involves extensive use of chemicals. The price tag for de-icing a wind turbine is equivalent to the value of two days' turbine production.}}</ref> or, in some cases, by helicopters or drones spraying clean warm water on the blades.<ref>{{cite web |title=Airborne de-icing solution for wind turbines |url=https://windren.se/WW2015/WW2015_13_312_Gedda_Deicing_helicopter.pdf |website=windren.se |access-date=17 March 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=De-icing wind turbines in Finland with KTV Working Drone |url=https://ktvworkingdrone.com/de-icing-wind-turbines-in-finland-with-ktv-working-drone/ |website=ktvworkingdrone.com |access-date=17 March 2026 |date=15 March 2024}}</ref>

Modern turbines usually have a small onboard [[Crane (machine)|crane]] for hoisting maintenance tools and minor components. However, large, heavy components like generators, gearboxes, blades, and so on are rarely replaced, and a [[Mobile crane|heavy lift external crane]] is needed in those cases. If the turbine has a difficult access road, a [[Liftra|containerized crane]] can be lifted up by the internal crane to provide heavier lifting.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ing.dk/artikel/dansk-firma-saetter-prisbeloennet-selvhejsende-kran-serieproduktion-184423 |title=Dansk firma sætter prisbelønnet selvhejsende kran i serieproduktion |author=Morten Lund |website=[[Ingeniøren]] |date=30 May 2016 |access-date=30 May 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160531115231/https://ing.dk/artikel/dansk-firma-saetter-prisbelonnet-selvhejsende-kran-i-serieproduktion-184423 |archive-date=31 May 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Repowering ===
{{main|Repowering}}
Installation of new wind turbines can be controversial. An alternative is repowering, where existing wind turbines are replaced with bigger, more powerful ones, sometimes in smaller numbers while keeping or increasing capacity.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wind Repowering Helps Set the Stage for Energy Transition |url=https://www.energy.gov/eere/wind/articles/wind-repowering-helps-set-stage-energy-transition |access-date=2023-05-23 |website=Energy.gov |date=6 May 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Demolition and recycling ===
Some wind turbines which are out of use are [[recycling|recycled]] or repowered.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.atlasobscura.com/articles/abandoned-dreams-of-wind-and-light |title=Abandoned Dreams of Wind and Light |author=Jeremy Fugleberg |date=8 May 2014 |website=Atlas Obscura |access-date=30 May 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.aweablog.org/fact-check-about-those-abandoned-turbines/ |title=Fact check: About those 'abandoned' turbines … |author=Tom Gray |publisher=[[American Wind Energy Association]] |date=11 March 2013 |access-date=30 May 2016 |archive-date=8 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160608233328/http://www.aweablog.org/fact-check-about-those-abandoned-turbines }}</ref> 85% of turbine materials are easily reused or recycled, but the blades, made of a composite material, are more difficult to process.<ref name=":2"/>

Interest in recycling blades varies in different markets and depends on the waste legislation and local economics. A challenge in recycling blades is related to the composite material, which is made of [[fiberglass]] with carbon fibers in epoxy resin, which cannot be remolded to form new composites.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2020-02-05 |title=Wind Turbine Blades Can't Be Recycled, So They're Piling Up in Landfills |language=en |work=Bloomberg.com |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/features/2020-02-05/wind-turbine-blades-can-t-be-recycled-so-they-re-piling-up-in-landfills |access-date=2023-06-07}}</ref>

Wind farm waste is less toxic than other garbage. Wind turbine blades represent only a fraction of overall waste in the US, according to the wind-industry [[trade association]], [[American Wind Energy Association]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=31 July 2019|title=Turbines Tossed Into Dump Stirs Debate on Wind's Dirty Downside|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-07-31/turbines-in-landfill-trigger-debate-over-wind-s-dirty-downside|access-date=6 December 2019|website=Bloomberg}}</ref>

Several utilities, startup companies, and researchers are developing methods for reusing or recycling blades.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|date=2020-10-30|title=Wind Turbine Blades Don't Have To End Up In Landfills|url=https://blog.ucsusa.org/james-gignac/wind-turbine-blades-recycling/|access-date=2022-01-23|website=The Equation|language=en-US}}</ref> Manufacturer [[Vestas]] has developed technology that can separate the fibers from the resin, allowing for reuse.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Barsoe|first=Tim|date=2021-05-17|title=End of wind power waste? Vestas unveils blade recycling technology|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/business/sustainable-business/end-wind-power-waste-vestas-unveils-blade-recycling-technology-2021-05-17/|access-date=2022-01-23}}</ref> In Germany, wind turbine blades are commercially recycled as part of an alternative fuel mix for a cement factory.<ref name=":2"/> In the United Kingdom, a project will trial cutting blades into strips for use as rebar in [[concrete]], with the aim of reducing emissions in the construction of [[High Speed 2]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=New HS2 pilot project swaps steel for retired wind turbine blades to reinforce concrete|url=https://mediacentre.hs2.org.uk/news/hs2-innovation-accelerator-company-pioneers-technology-to-cut-carbon-and-concrete-waste|access-date=2021-03-12|website=High Speed 2|language=en}}</ref> Used wind turbine blades have been recycled by incorporating them as part of the support structures within pedestrian bridges in Poland<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.compositesworld.com/news/anmet-installs-first-recycled-wind-turbine-blade-based-pedestrian-bridge |title=Anmet installs first recycled wind turbine blade-based pedestrian bridge |date=21 October 2021 |first=Hannah |last=Mason |work= CompositesWorld}}</ref> and Ireland.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.theverge.com/2022/2/11/22929059/recycled-wind-turbine-blade-bridges-world-first |title=Engineers are building bridges with recycled wind turbine blades |first=Maddie |last=Stone |date=11 February 2022 |work=[[The Verge]]}}</ref> In 2026, Chinese manufacturer [[Ming Yang Smart Energy|Ming Yang]] developed the first fully recyclable wind turbine, which uses [[Pultrusion|pultruded]] carbon fiber panels instead of fiberglass, allowing recyclers to separate the components through a chemical process.<ref>{{cite web |title=World's first 361-foot fully recyclable wind turbine blade unveiled in China |url=https://interestingengineering.com/energy/china-worlds-first-fully-recyclable-wind-turbine-blade |website=interestingengineering.com |access-date=12 March 2026 |date=8 January 2026}}</ref>

== Comparison with other power sources ==

=== Advantages ===

Wind turbines is one of the lowest-cost sources of renewable energy along with [[solar panel]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-07-13 |title=Renewable Power Remains Cost-Competitive amid Fossil Fuel Crisis |url=https://www.irena.org/news/pressreleases/2022/Jul/Renewable-Power-Remains-Cost-Competitive-amid-Fossil-Fuel-Crisis |access-date=2023-05-19 |website=www.irena.org |language=en}}</ref> As technology needed for wind turbines continued to improve, the prices decreased as well. In addition, there is currently no competitive market for wind energy (though there may be in the future), because wind is a freely available natural resource, most of which is untapped.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=2013-06-19 |title=Advantages and Disadvantages of Wind Energy – Clean Energy Ideas |language=en |work=Clean Energy Ideas |url=http://www.clean-energy-ideas.com/wind/wind-energy/advantages-and-disadvantages-of-wind-energy |access-date=2017-05-10}}</ref> The main cost of small wind turbines is the purchase and installation process, which averages between $48,000 and $65,000 per installation. Usually, the total amount of energy harvested amounts to more than the cost of the turbines.<ref>{{Cite web |title=WINDExchange: Economics and Incentives for Wind |url=https://windexchange.energy.gov/projects/economics |access-date=2023-05-19 |website=windexchange.energy.gov}}</ref>

Wind turbines provide a clean energy source,<ref name="rue21" /> use little water,<ref name=evans2009/> emitting no greenhouse gases and no waste products during operation. Over {{convert|1,500|ST|t|order=flip}} of carbon dioxide per year can be eliminated by using a one-megawatt turbine instead of one megawatt of energy from a fossil fuel.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url= http://www.pawindenergynow.org/wind/facts.html|title=About Wind Energy: Factsheets and Statistics|website=www.pawindenergynow.org |access-date=2017-05-10}}</ref>

=== Disadvantages ===
[[File:2017 Human-related causes of bird deaths (US).svg|thumb|In the U.S. cats kill on the order of 10,000 times as many birds as [[wind turbines]].<ref name=FWSbirdDeaths>{{cite web |title=Threats to Birds / Top Threats to Birds (U.S. only. Ordered by Median Estimate of Bird Mortality Annually. As of 2017.) |url=https://www.fws.gov/library/collections/threats-birds |publisher=U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250213033928/https://www.fws.gov/library/collections/threats-birds |archive-date=13 February 2025 |date=2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>]]

[[Environmental impact of wind power]] includes effect on wildlife, but can be mitigated if proper strategies are implemented.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Parisé | first1 = J. | last2 = Walker | first2 = T. R. | year = 2017 | title = Industrial wind turbine post-construction bird and bat monitoring: A policy framework for Canada | journal = Journal of Environmental Management | volume = 201 | pages = 252–259 | doi=10.1016/j.jenvman.2017.06.052| pmid = 28672197  | bibcode = 2017JEnvM.201..252P }}</ref> Thousands of birds, including rare species, have been killed by the blades of wind turbines,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hosansky|first=David|date=1 April 2011|title=Wind Power: Is wind energy good for the environment?|journal=CQ Researcher}}</ref> though wind turbines contribute relatively insignificantly to anthropogenic avian mortality (birds killed by humans). Wind farms and [[nuclear power plant]]s are responsible for between 0.3 and 0.4 bird deaths per gigawatt-hour (GWh) of electricity while [[fossil fuel power station]]s are responsible for about 5.2 fatalities per GWh. In comparison, conventional coal-fired generators contribute significantly more to bird mortality.<ref>{{Cite web |title=How Harmful is Renewable Energy to Birds? |url=https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/how-harmful-is-renewable-energy-to-birds |access-date=2023-06-02 |website=www.eesi.org}}</ref> A study on recorded bird populations in the United States from 2000 to 2020 found the presence of wind turbines had no significant effect on bird population numbers.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Katovich |first1=Erik |title=Quantifying the Effects of Energy Infrastructure on Bird Populations and Biodiversity |journal=Environmental Science & Technology |date=9 January 2024 |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=323–332 |doi=10.1021/acs.est.3c03899 |pmid=38153963 |bibcode=2024EnST...58..323K }}</ref>

Energy harnessed by wind turbines is variable, and is not a "dispatchable" source of power; its availability is based on whether the wind is blowing, not whether electricity is needed. Turbines can be placed on [[ridge]]s or [[bluff (geography)|bluff]]s to maximize the access of wind they have, but this also limits the locations where they can be placed.<ref name=":0" /> In this way, wind energy is not a particularly reliable source of energy. However, it can form part of the [[energy mix]], which also includes power from other sources. Technology is also being developed to store excess energy, which can then make up for any deficits in supplies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Grid-Scale Storage – Analysis |url=https://www.iea.org/reports/grid-scale-storage |access-date=2023-06-02 |website=IEA}}</ref>

{{anchor|ADLS|adls}}
Wind turbines have [[Aviation obstruction lighting|blinking lights]] that warn aircraft, to avoid collisions.<ref name=Electrek_20230929/> Residents living near windfarms, especially those in rural areas, have complained that the blinking lights are a bothersome form of [[light pollution]].<ref name=Electrek_20230929/> A light mitigation approach involves Aircraft Detection Lighting Systems (ADLSs) by which the lights are turned on, only when the ADLS's [[radar]] detects aircraft within thresholds of altitude and distance.<ref name=Electrek_20230929>{{cite news |last1=Lewis |first1=Michelle |title=A new wind farm in Kansas trailblazes with light-mitigating technology |url=https://electrek.co/2023/09/29/a-new-wind-farm-in-kansas-trailblazes-with-light-mitigating-technology/ |publisher=Electrek |date=29 September 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230929161033/https://electrek.co/2023/09/29/a-new-wind-farm-in-kansas-trailblazes-with-light-mitigating-technology/ |archive-date=29 September 2023 |url-status=live }}</ref>
